questions.hint: Look for a solubility limit that changes with temperature and a way to retain excess solute temporarily.
questions.explanation: Age hardening requires a suitable alloy with greater solid solubility at the solution-treatment temperature. Solution treatment dissolves particles; rapid cooling retains a supersaturated solution; aging allows fine precipitates to develop. Those particles obstruct dislocation motion. Natural aging occurs near room temperature and artificial aging at a higher controlled temperature. This mechanism differs from diffusionless martensite formation.
questions.misconception: The sequence is dissolution, retained supersaturation, then controlled precipitation. A pure metal or an unsuitable phase diagram cannot automatically be age hardened.
optionReasons: Softening can occur after excessive aging; it is not the initial precipitation-strengthening objective. For this question, that alternative does not satisfy the required relationship. The sequence is dissolution, retained supersaturation, then controlled precipitation. A pure metal or an unsuitable phase diagram cannot automatically be age hardened.

questions.hint: Consider what rapid cooling prevents carbon from doing before the lattice changes shape.
questions.explanation: Martensite forms through a rapid diffusionless lattice distortion. Carbon is trapped, producing the body-centered-tetragonal structure in carbon steel rather than equilibrium ferrite plus carbide. Carbon increases the distortion and generally raises hardness. The martensite fraction depends strongly on the lowest temperature reached. Tempering subsequently lets carbon redistribute and usually trades some hardness for improved toughness.

questions.hint: Follow the precipitates from their earliest state through the strongest dispersion to coarsening.
questions.explanation: An underaged alloy has an insufficiently developed precipitate population. Peak aging produces an effective size and spacing of obstacles. Overaging coarsens particles and often lowers strength. Coherent particles maintain lattice continuity with the matrix and can create substantial strain fields. Loss of coherency and changes in spacing alter how dislocations interact with particles. Time and temperature therefore jointly control strength.
questions.misconception: Longer aging is not always stronger. Coherent and incoherent interfaces differ in lattice matching; a large particle is not necessarily a better strengthening obstacle.

questions.hint: Consider what rapid cooling prevents carbon from doing before the lattice changes shape.
questions.explanation: Martensite forms through a rapid diffusionless lattice distortion. Carbon is trapped, producing the body-centered-tetragonal structure in carbon steel rather than equilibrium ferrite plus carbide. Carbon increases the distortion and generally raises hardness. The martensite fraction depends strongly on the lowest temperature reached. Tempering subsequently lets carbon redistribute and usually trades some hardness for improved toughness.

questions.hint: Identify the backbone and then the side group attached to it.

questions.explanation: Metals have accessible nearby electronic states; semiconductors have a small gap and insulators usually a larger gap. Thermal excitation in a semiconductor creates conduction electrons and valence-band holes. In metals, thermal vibrations, impurities and deformation defects scatter carriers and usually reduce conductivity. In intrinsic semiconductors, heating creates more carriers and generally raises conductivity despite mobility changes.
